docs.title: Welcome to the Open Source AI Learning Hub
Our Mission
docs.text:
The AI Learning Hub is an open-source initiative dedicated to building the ultimate resource for learning AI, machine learning, and Python programming. Whether you're a beginner or an advanced learner, our goal is to provide high-quality, accessible, and continuously evolving educational content that empowers everyone to master AI technologies.

This is more than a learning platform—it's a community-driven project. Together, we’re shaping the future of AI education.

docs.title: Building the AI Learning Roadmap
docs.text:
At the heart of this initiative is the AI Learning Roadmap—a structured guide that takes learners from fundamental programming skills to advanced AI topics.

The roadmap is organized into distinct sections:

  • Programming: Covering Python and other programming languages relevant to AI.
  • Working with Data: Introducing tools like Pandas, NumPy, and data visualization libraries.
  • Machine Learning: Teaching core algorithms, evaluation metrics, and tuning techniques.
  • Deep Learning: Exploring neural networks, advanced architectures, and applications.
  • MLOps and Model Deployment: Bridging the gap between experimentation and production.

We’re inviting contributors to help us create, improve, and expand tutorials in each of these sections. Every tutorial you add strengthens this roadmap and helps learners worldwide master the concepts.

docs.title: How to Contribute to the AI Learning Hub 🛠️
docs.text: We’re thrilled that you’re interested in contributing to the AI Learning Hub! This guide will walk you through the steps to make your contributions seamless. Whether you’re submitting new tutorials, fixing bugs, or suggesting improvements, your efforts make a difference.

docs.title: Step 1: Familiarize Yourself with the Project
docs.text:
Before contributing, take some time to:

  • Explore the GitHub repository.
  • Understand the structure of the project and where your contribution fits.
  • Review any open issues or pull requests to avoid duplication.

docs.title: Step 2: Create or Select an Issue
docs.text:
1. Check for Existing Issues:

    • Browse the Issues section to see if your idea or task is already listed.
    • If you find an issue you'd like to work on, comment on it to let the maintainers know you're taking it up. Example comment: "I’d like to work on this issue. Please assign it to me!"

    • Create a New Issue:

    • If your contribution is new and not listed, create a detailed issue describing your idea or proposed feature.

    • Include as much information as possible, such as the content type, purpose, and scope.
    • Wait for approval from the maintainers before proceeding.

👉 Submit or Review Issues Here

docs.title: Step 3: Fork the Repository
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the AI Learning Hub GitHub repository.
  2. Click the Fork button in the top-right corner to create a personal copy of the repository.

docs.title: Step 4: Clone Your Fork
docs.text:
1. Open your terminal or command prompt.

  2. Clone your forked repository to your local machine by running:

    git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/ailearninghub.git

    Replace <your-username> with your GitHub username.

docs.title: Step 5: Set Up Your Development Environment
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the project directory:

    cd ailearninghub

  2. Create a virtual environment:

    python -m venv env

  3. Activate the virtual environment:

    • On Windows:

      .\env\Scripts\activate

    • On macOS/Linux:

      source env/bin/activate

  4. Install the required Python libraries:

    pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Step 6: Make Your Changes
docs.text:
• Add or edit content, code, or documentation based on the approved issue or feature request.
  • Follow the existing project structure and style guides.
  • Test your changes locally to ensure everything works as expected.

docs.title: Creating Tutorials
docs.text:
1. Use the Python Basics Template: When creating a new tutorial, base your tutorial off the Python Basics tutorial located at:

    docs/ai_learning_roadmap/0_programming/python/basics.ipynb

    This ensures consistency in structure and formatting.

  2. Place Your Tutorial Correctly: Save your tutorial in the appropriate category and subdirectory, similar to how the Python Basics tutorial is structured.

  3. Add Your Tutorial to the mkdocs.yml File: Once your tutorial is created, you need to add it to the mkdocs.yml file for it to appear in the website navigation. Follow these steps:

    • Open the mkdocs.yml file in the root directory of the project.
    • Locate the section corresponding to your tutorial's category (e.g., Programming, Working with Data).

    • Add your tutorial under the appropriate subcategory, following the same format as the Python Basics file:

      - Programming:
    - "[Contribute]": 'ai_learning_roadmap/0_programming/contribute.md'
    - Python:
        - Basics: 'ai_learning_roadmap/0_programming/python/basics.ipynb'
        - Your Tutorial Title: 'path/to/your/tutorial/file.ipynb'

    • Use the example in the image below for guidance:

    • Ensure the file path matches the directory where your tutorial is saved.

docs.title: Step 7: Preview Your Changes Locally
docs.text:
Before creating a pull request, ensure your changes render correctly by using mkdocs:

  1. Start the development server:

    mkdocs serve

  2. Open the provided URL in your browser (usually http://127.0.0.1:8000) to preview your changes.

  3. Verify that everything looks and functions as expected.

docs.title: Step 8: Commit Your Changes
docs.text:
1. Stage your changes:

    git add .

  2. Commit your changes with a meaningful message:

    git commit -m "Add/Update [description of your changes]"

docs.title: Step 9: Push to Your Fork
docs.text:
Push your branch to your forked repository:

git push origin feature/your-feature-name

docs.title: Step 10: Create a Pull Request
docs.text:
1. Go to the original AI Learning Hub repository.
  2. Click the Pull Requests tab, then click New Pull Request.
  3. Select Compare Across Forks.
  4. Set the base repository to dankornas/ailearninghub and the compare repository to your fork.
  5. Add a clear title and description of your changes, referencing the approved issue number (e.g., "Fixes #42").
  6. Confirm that you’ve previewed your changes locally using mkdocs serve and include this note in your pull request description.
  7. Submit the pull request.

docs.title: Step 11: Collaborate and Refine
docs.text:
• The maintainers will review your pull request.
  • Be open to feedback and make necessary adjustments.

docs.title: Step 12: Celebrate Your Contribution! 🎉
docs.text: Once your pull request is merged, your contribution becomes part of the AI Learning Hub! Share your achievement with the community.

docs.title: Additional Tips
docs.text:
• Ask Questions: If you’re unsure about anything, ask in our Discord Community.

  • Be Respectful: Follow the Contributor Code of Conduct to ensure a welcoming environment for all contributors.

  • Stay Updated: Keep your fork in sync with the original repository by pulling updates regularly:

    git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main

We’re excited to have you on board! Together, we’re building something extraordinary for the AI community.

docs.title: How to Create Tutorials for the AI Learning Hub 📝
docs.text: Thank you for contributing to the AI Learning Hub! This guide explains how to create tutorials that fit seamlessly into the project. By following these steps, we can maintain consistency, organization, and high-quality content.

docs.title: Step 1: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you start working on your tutorial:

  1. Create or Select an Issue: Ensure you’ve created or selected an issue in the GitHub Issues section and received approval to proceed.
  2. Set Up Your Environment: Follow the How to Contribute guide to set up your development environment, including installing dependencies and activating your virtual environment.

docs.title: Step 2: File Structure
docs.text:
After your issue has been approved and you’re ready to start, you’ll need to create a new file in the appropriate directory under ai-learning-roadmap. The directory structure is as follows:

docs/
└── ai-learning-roadmap/
    ├── 0_programming/
    ├── 1_working_with_data/
    ├── 2_machine_learning/
    ├── 3_deep_learning/
    └── 4_mlop_deployment/
  • Choose the directory that best matches your tutorial topic:
    • 0_programming: Tutorials on programming fundamentals like Python, algorithms, and basic data structures.
    • 1_working_with_data: Tutorials on working with data, including data cleaning, Pandas, NumPy, and visualization.
    • 2_machine_learning: Tutorials on machine learning models, algorithms, and workflows.
    • 3_deep_learning: Tutorials on neural networks, advanced AI techniques, and frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch.
    • 4_mlop_deployment: Tutorials on deploying machine learning models, pipelines, and MLOps best practices.

docs.title: Step 3: Working with Jupyter Notebooks
docs.text: The tutorials in this project will primarily be created using Jupyter Notebooks (.ipynb files). MkDocs-Jupyter will render these notebooks as interactive pages, so it’s important to follow formatting conventions to ensure proper rendering.

docs.title: How to Create and Save Your Notebook
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the directory where your tutorial will live (e.g., docs/ai-learning-roadmap/2_machine_learning).

  2. Open Jupyter Notebook or Jupyter Lab in your terminal:

    jupyter notebook

  3. Create a new notebook and save it with a descriptive name, such as:

    tutorial_name.ipynb

  4. Add your content using the structure outlined below.

docs.title: Step 4: Formatting Standards
docs.text: When using MkDocs-Jupyter, you’ll need to follow specific formatting conventions to ensure the notebook renders correctly. Here’s a breakdown:

docs.title: Markdown Cells
docs.text:
Use markdown cells for explanations, headings, and structured text. Below are some formatting guidelines:

  • Headings: Use markdown syntax for section headers.
    • # Main Title
    • ## Section Title
    • ### Subsection Title
  • Text Emphasis:
    • Italics: Surround text with single asterisks or underscores: _italic text_ or *italic text*
    • Bold: Surround text with double asterisks: **bold text**
    • Bold Italics: Combine both: ***bold italic text***

  • Bullet Points: Use - or * for unordered lists:

    - First item
- Second item

  • Numbered Lists: Use numbers for ordered lists:

    1. Step one
2. Step two

  • Links: Use [text](url) to create hyperlinks:

    [GitHub Repository](https://github.com/dankornas/ailearninghub)

  • Inline Code: Use backticks for inline code:

    Use `print()` to display output in Python.

docs.title: Code Cells
docs.text:
Use Python code cells for any programming examples or exercises. MkDocs-Jupyter renders these as executable cells. Ensure the following:

  1. Include relevant comments for clarity:

    # This function adds two numbers
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

  2. Provide input/output examples where possible:

    result = add(5, 10)
print(result)  # Output: 15

  3. Keep code concise and avoid overly complex examples.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
You can create tables in markdown cells for structured data:

| Parameter | Description     | Example  |
|-----------|-----------------|----------|
| Name      | The user's name | John Doe |
| Age       | User's age      | 25       |

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
Add images by linking them with markdown syntax:

![Alt Text](path/to/image.png)

docs.title: Tips and Notes
docs.text:
Use blockquotes for additional tips, notes, or warnings:

> **Note:** Ensure your Python version matches the required dependencies.

docs.title: Step 5: Add Author Information
docs.text: While creating your tutorial or immediately after, include a section at the end of your Jupyter notebook to provide information about yourself. This helps recognize contributors and builds a sense of community.

docs.title: Template for Author Information
docs.text:
At the end of your Jupyter notebook, add the following markdown cell:

---

## About the Author

This tutorial was created by **Your Name**.

- **GitHub**: [@your-github-username](https://github.com/your-github-username)
- **LinkedIn**: [Your LinkedIn Profile](https://linkedin.com/in/your-profile)
- **Twitter**: [@your-twitter-handle](https://twitter.com/your-twitter-handle) (optional)

If you have any questions or feedback, feel free to reach out or submit an issue in the [AI Learning Hub GitHub repository](https://github.com/dankornas/ailearninghub).

---

docs.title: Step 6: Content Guidelines
docs.text:
• Write tutorials in simple, clear, and engaging language.
  • Structure your tutorial into sections:
    1. Introduction: Briefly explain the topic and what learners will achieve.
    2. Prerequisites: List any tools, libraries, or knowledge needed.
    3. Step-by-Step Guide: Explain each step clearly with examples.
    4. Conclusion: Summarize the key takeaways and encourage further exploration.
  • Use real-world examples whenever possible to demonstrate practical applications.
  • Avoid overly long sections—break content into digestible chunks.

docs.title: Step 7: Testing and Previewing
docs.text:
Before submitting your tutorial:

  1. Run your Jupyter notebook end-to-end to ensure:
    • All code runs without errors.
    • Outputs match what’s expected.

  2. Use the mkdocs serve command to preview your tutorial locally:

    mkdocs serve

  3. Open the provided URL (usually http://127.0.0.1:8000) to verify formatting and readability.

docs.title: Step 8: Submit Your Tutorial
docs.text:
Once your tutorial is complete and tested:

  • Commit your changes with a descriptive message.
  • Create a pull request and link it to your issue.
  • Be open to feedback from maintainers to refine your work.

Thank you for contributing to the AI Learning Hub and helping us create a world-class learning resource! 🚀

docs.title: Get Started with the AI Learning Roadmap 🚀
docs.text: Welcome to the AI Learning Roadmap! This step-by-step guide will help you navigate through the roadmap, build a strong foundation, and advance your skills in programming, working with data, machine learning, and deep learning. Follow the sections in order to get the most out of the roadmap.

docs.title: How to Use the AI Learning Roadmap
docs.text:
The roadmap is structured to guide you from basic programming skills to advanced AI and machine learning concepts. Here's how to go through each section:

  1. Start with Programming Fundamentals: Build your foundational knowledge of Python.
  2. Learn to Work with Data: Explore libraries like Pandas, Matplotlib, Seaborn, and NumPy to manipulate, analyze, and visualize data.
  3. Dive into Machine Learning: Understand the fundamentals of machine learning and master algorithms, evaluation metrics, and hyperparameter tuning.
  4. Advance to Deep Learning: Build and train neural networks, and apply concepts like CNNs, RNNs, and GANs using TensorFlow and Keras.
  5. Move on to MLOps and Model Deployment: Apply your skills to deploy and manage models in production environments.

docs.title: Programming - Join Us as a Contributor!
docs.text:
The AI Learning Hub Open Source platform invites you to contribute to the Programming section. This section lays the foundation for understanding programming and scripting languages essential for machine learning, deep learning, and data science. Strong programming skills are critical for building, training, and deploying AI models effectively.

We’re looking for contributors to create or enhance tutorials on programming concepts, not only in Python but also in other relevant programming or scripting languages. Together, we can help learners worldwide master the tools they need to succeed in AI.

docs.title: Example Topics We’d Like to Cover
docs.text: Below are some example topics that highlight the kinds of tutorials we’d like to include. These are just suggestions, and we welcome additional ideas and contributions to expand the section!

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
• Basics:
    • Data Types & Variables
    • Loops & Iterators
    • Functions & Lambdas
    • Lists
    • Conditionals
    • Tuples
    • Dictionaries
    • Sets
    • Strings
    • Map and Filter
    • Exception Handling
  • Object-Oriented Programming:
    • Classes
    • Inheritance & Polymorphism
    • Encapsulation
    • Magic Methods

docs.title: Other Relevant Programming Languages
docs.text:
We encourage tutorials on programming languages and tools that complement Python or are widely used in machine learning and deep learning workflows:

  • R: Data manipulation, visualization, and statistical modeling.
  • Julia: High-performance numerical and scientific computing.
  • Bash: Automating workflows, scripting, and environment setup.

docs.title: Cross-Language Topics
docs.text:
• Best practices for transitioning between programming languages.
  • Writing interoperable code (e.g., Python-C++ integration).
  • Performance optimization using multiple programming tools.

docs.title: How You Can Contribute
docs.text:
1. Create Tutorials: Develop beginner-friendly, step-by-step guides to explain programming concepts. Include code examples and practical use cases to make the tutorials engaging and hands-on.
  2. Expand Language Coverage: Contribute tutorials on languages beyond Python that are relevant for machine learning and deep learning workflows.
  3. Enhance Existing Tutorials: Add additional examples, improve clarity, or expand on advanced topics within the programming section.
  4. Suggest New Topics: Identify key programming concepts or techniques we should include.
  5. Provide Code Examples: Share code snippets, scripts, or Jupyter Notebooks to support your tutorials.
  6. Community Support: Help answer questions, provide feedback, or mentor learners in our community forums and Discord.

docs.title: Why Contribute?
docs.text:
• Impact: Help learners worldwide build strong programming foundations for AI and data science.
  • Recognition: Be acknowledged as a contributor on our platform and within the community.
  • Skill Development: Enhance your programming knowledge while contributing to open-source education.
  • Networking: Collaborate with other contributors and connect with professionals passionate about AI.

docs.title: Python Classes and Objects¶
docs.text: Python is an object-oriented programming (OOP) language, which means it allows programmers to create objects that encapsulate data and functionality together. Understanding classes and objects is essential for writing efficient and organized Python code.

docs.title: Understanding Classes and Objects¶
docs.text:
Class: A blueprint or template for creating objects. It defines a set of attributes and methods that the instantiated objects (instances) will have.

Object: An instance of a class. It is a real-world entity that has properties (attributes) and behaviors (methods).

docs.title: Defining a Class¶
docs.text:
Defining a class in Python is straightforward.

  • Class Name: Should follow the PascalCase naming convention (each word capitalized, no underscores).
  • Class Body: Contains method definitions and variables.

If you don’t want to add any attributes or methods immediately, you can use the pass statement to define an empty class.

docs.title: The init Method (Constructor)¶
docs.text:
The init method is a special method called a constructor.

It is automatically invoked when a new instance of the class is created. It initializes the object’s attributes.

self: Refers to the instance of the class. It is used to access class attributes and methods.

docs.title: Instance Variables and Class Variables¶
docs.text:
Instance Variables

  • Defined within methods.
  • Unique to each instance.
  • Prefixed with self.

Class Variables

  • Defined within the class but outside any methods.
  • Shared among all instances of the class.

docs.title: Methods in Classes¶
docs.text:
Methods are functions defined inside a class that describe the behaviors of an object.

class ClassName:
    def method_name(self, parameters):
        # method body

self: Always the first parameter. It refers to the instance calling the method.

docs.title: Accessing Attributes and Methods¶
docs.text:
You can access an object’s attributes and methods using the dot . notation.

Accessing Attributes

object.attribute

Accessing Methods

object.method()

docs.title: Modifying Attributes¶
docs.text: You can modify an object’s attributes directly or via methods.

docs.title: Encapsulation¶
docs.text: Encapsulation is the concept of bundling data and methods within a class and restricting direct access to some of the object’s components.

docs.title: Private Attributes¶
docs.text:
In Python, private attributes are indicated by prefixing the attribute name with an underscore _ or double underscore __.

  • Single Underscore (_variable): Suggests that the variable is intended for internal use.
  • Double Underscore (__variable): Triggers name mangling to prevent accidental access.

docs.text: Exception handling in Python involves intercepting errors during the execution of a program and taking corrective or alternative actions rather than letting the program crash. This is done using try-except blocks, among other tools.

docs.title: Exception Handling in Real Scenarios¶
docs.text: Exception handling is particularly useful in data input/output operations, network operations, and handling unexpected behaviors in data-driven applications. docs.title: Best Practices¶
docs.text:
• Catch specific exceptions: Whenever possible, catch more specific exceptions rather than a general Exception class.

docs.title: Python Variables¶
docs.text: Python variables are like containers that store data values, allowing you to label and reference that data throughout your code. They let you assign and reassign values, making it easier to manage and manipulate information as your program runs.

docs.title: Naming Variable¶
docs.text: The simplest way to describe variables is that they are names that are assigned to values. These names can start with either a letter or an underscore, but not a number.

docs.title: Case Sensitive Variables¶
docs.text: Variable names are case sensitive, meaning two variables with the same name but one has an uppercase letter will be treated differently than the variable with the lowercase letter.

docs.title: Casting Data Types¶
docs.text: Casting allows you want to change a variable's data type to a different type. For example, if you want to change the type of a variable, which is a float, into an integer, you would use int().

array_1d = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])
# Creating a 1D array from a list array_1d = np.array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

array_2d = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])
# Creating a 2D array from a list of lists array_2d = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])

Here, array_2d is a 2x3 matrix with two rows and three columns. This structure allows you to perform operations like matrix multiplication and transposition.

In [4]: Copied!

array_3d = np.array([
    [[1, 2], [3, 4]],
    [[5, 6], [7, 8]]
])
# Creating a 3D array array_3d = np.array([ [[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[5, 6], [7, 8]] ])

In this example, array_3d is a three-dimensional array with dimensions 2x2x2. This kind of array is useful in advanced computations like those found in machine learning and scientific simulations.

In [5]: Copied! 
array = np.array([[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]])

# Number of dimensions
num_dimensions = array.ndim

# Shape of the array

# Total number of elements
total_elements = array.size

# Data type of elements

In the code above, you can inspect these attributes to understand the array's properties, which is particularly useful when debugging or performing operations that require arrays of specific shapes and types.

In [6]: Copied! 
# Creating a 1D array of zeros with 5 elements
zeros_1d = np.zeros(5)

# Creating a 2D array of zeros with 3 rows and 4 columns
zeros_2d = np.zeros((3, 4))
# Creating a 1D array of zeros with 5 elements zeros_1d = np.zeros(5) # Creating a 2D array of zeros with 3 rows and 4 columns zeros_2d = np.zeros((3, 4))

In these examples, zeros_1d is a one-dimensional array of five zeros, and zeros_2d is a two-dimensional array with three rows and four columns, all initialized to zero.

In [7]: Copied!

ones_1d = np.ones(5)

# Creating a 2D array of ones with 2 rows and 3 columns
ones_2d = np.ones((2, 3))
# Creating a 1D array of ones with 5 elements ones_1d = np.ones(5) # Creating a 2D array of ones with 2 rows and 3 columns ones_2d = np.ones((2, 3))

These arrays, ones_1d and ones_2d, can serve as initial matrices or vectors in various mathematical computations.

In [8]: Copied! 
# Creating a 2D array filled with the value 7
constant_array = np.full((3, 3), 7)
# Creating a 2D array filled with the value 7 constant_array = np.full((3, 3), 7)

In this example, constant_array is a 3x3 matrix where every element is the integer 7.

In [9]: Copied! 
# Creating a 4x4 identity matrix using np.identity()
identity_matrix = np.identity(4)

# Creating a 4x4 identity matrix using np.eye()
eye_matrix = np.eye(4)
# Creating a 4x4 identity matrix using np.identity() identity_matrix = np.identity(4) # Creating a 4x4 identity matrix using np.eye() eye_matrix = np.eye(4)

Both identity_matrix and eye_matrix are 4x4 matrices with ones on the diagonal from the top-left to the bottom-right corner.

You can also multiply the identity matrix by a scalar to adjust the values along the diagonal:

In [10]: Copied!

# Scaling the identity matrix by 5 scaled_identity = np.eye(4) * 5

Here, scaled_identity is an identity matrix with the diagonal elements scaled by 5, resulting in a matrix with fives on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere.

# Creating an array from 5 to 50 with a step of 5
step_array = np.arange(5, 55, 5)
# Creating an array from 0 to 9 range_array = np.arange(10) # Creating an array from 5 to 50 with a step of 5 step_array = np.arange(5, 55, 5)

In the first example, range_array contains numbers from 0 to 9. In the second example, step_array contains numbers from 5 to 50 in increments of 5.

In [12]: Copied! 
# Generating 5 numbers between 0 and 1
linspace_array = np.linspace(0, 1, 5)

# Generating 10 numbers between 0 and 100
linspace_array_10 = np.linspace(0, 100, 10)
# Generating 5 numbers between 0 and 1 linspace_array = np.linspace(0, 1, 5) # Generating 10 numbers between 0 and 100 linspace_array_10 = np.linspace(0, 100, 10)

Here, linspace_array creates an array of five numbers evenly spaced between 0 and 1, while linspace_array_10 creates an array of ten numbers evenly spaced between 0 and 100.

In [13]: Copied! 
# Generating a 1D array of 5 random floats between 0 and 1
random_array = np.random.rand(5)

# Generating a 2D array of random floats between 0 and 1
random_array_2d = np.random.rand(3, 4)

# Generating a 1D array of 5 random integers between 10 and 50
random_int_array = np.random.randint(10, 50, 5)
# Generating a 1D array of 5 random floats between 0 and 1 random_array = np.random.rand(5) # Generating a 2D array of random floats between 0 and 1 random_array_2d = np.random.rand(3, 4) # Generating a 1D array of 5 random integers between 10 and 50 random_int_array = np.random.randint(10, 50, 5)

Each time you run these functions, they produce different random values. If you need reproducible results, you can set the random seed using np.random.seed().

In [14]: Copied! 
# Setting the seed for reproducibility
np.random.seed(42)

# Generating random numbers after setting the seed
seeded_random_array = np.random.rand(5)
# Setting the seed for reproducibility np.random.seed(42) # Generating random numbers after setting the seed seeded_random_array = np.random.rand(5)

By setting the seed, you ensure that the random numbers generated are the same every time you run the code, which is essential for debugging and consistent results in experiments.

docs.title: NumPy Basics: Creating Arrays¶
docs.text: NumPy is a fundamental library for scientific computing in Python, providing support for arrays and matrices, along with a collection of mathematical functions to operate on them efficiently.

docs.title: Introduction to NumPy Arrays¶
docs.text:
NumPy arrays are the core of the NumPy library. They are similar to Python lists but come with added benefits:

  • Efficiency: NumPy arrays are more compact and faster than Python lists.
  • Functionality: They support vectorized operations, allowing for element-wise operations without explicit loops.
  • Dimensionality: They can be multi-dimensional, enabling complex mathematical computations.

Understanding how to create and manipulate NumPy arrays is fundamental for scientific computing and data analysis in Python.

docs.title: Importing NumPy¶
docs.text: Before you start working with NumPy, you need to import the library into your Python environment. It's a common practice to import NumPy using the alias np, which makes it easier to reference the library's functions.

docs.title: Creating Arrays from Lists and Tuples¶
docs.text: One of the simplest ways to create a NumPy array is from a Python list or tuple using the np.array() function.

docs.title: One-Dimensional Arrays¶
docs.text: A one-dimensional array, also known as a vector, can be created by passing a list or tuple of numbers to np.array(). This array will act similarly to a list but with additional functionalities provided by NumPy.

docs.title: Two-Dimensional Arrays¶
docs.text: To create a two-dimensional array, or matrix, you can pass a list of lists (or tuples of tuples) to np.array(). Each inner list represents a row in the matrix.

docs.title: Higher-Dimensional Arrays¶
docs.text: NumPy also supports arrays with more than two dimensions, known as multi-dimensional arrays or tensors. You can create these by nesting lists or tuples further.

docs.title: Array Attributes¶
docs.text:
NumPy arrays come with several attributes that provide information about the array's structure and data. Understanding these attributes can help you manipulate arrays more effectively.

  • ndim: The number of dimensions (axes) of the array.
  • shape: A tuple indicating the size of the array in each dimension.
  • size: The total number of elements in the array.
  • dtype: The data type of the array's elements.

docs.title: Generating Arrays Using NumPy Functions¶
docs.text: NumPy provides several functions to create arrays with specific patterns or values, which can be highly efficient for initializing arrays without manually specifying each element.

docs.title: Arrays of Zeros¶
docs.text: To create an array filled entirely with zeros, you can use the np.zeros() function. This is often used as a starting point in algorithms where you need a placeholder array.

docs.title: Arrays of Ones¶
docs.text: Similarly, you can create an array filled with ones using the np.ones() function. This is useful in situations where you need an array initialized with ones, such as in certain normalization processes.

docs.title: Constant Arrays¶
docs.text: If you need an array filled with a specific constant value, you can use the np.full() function. This is particularly handy when a particular value is required for initialization.

docs.title: Identity and Eye Arrays¶
docs.text:
Identity matrices are square matrices with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere. NumPy provides two functions to create such matrices:

  • np.identity(n): Creates an n x n identity matrix.
  • np.eye(N, M=None, k=0): Creates a 2-D array with ones on the k-th diagonal.

docs.title: Arrays with a Range of Values¶
docs.text: NumPy offers functions to create arrays with sequences of numbers, which is useful for generating indices or ranges of values for calculations.

docs.title: Using arange()¶
docs.text: The np.arange() function creates an array with evenly spaced values within a specified interval. It works similarly to Python's built-in range() function but returns a NumPy array.

docs.title: Using linspace()¶
docs.text: The np.linspace() function generates a specified number of evenly spaced values over a given interval. This is particularly useful in scientific computations where you need to sample a function at evenly spaced points.

docs.title: Random Arrays¶
docs.text:
NumPy's random module allows you to generate arrays with random numbers, which can be useful for simulations, random sampling, and initializing algorithms.

  • np.random.rand(): Generates an array of the given shape with random samples from a uniform distribution over [0, 1).
  • np.random.randn(): Generates samples from the standard normal distribution (mean 0, variance 1).
  • np.random.randint(): Generates random integers between a low (inclusive) and high (exclusive) value.

docs.title: NumPy Data Manipulation Tutorial¶
docs.text: NumPy offers a variety of functions for manipulating arrays, allowing you to reshape, join, split, and modify data efficiently. Mastering these data manipulation techniques is essential for data analysis, machine learning, and scientific computing.

docs.title: 2. Importing NumPy¶
docs.text: Before you start working with NumPy, you need to import the library. It's standard practice to import NumPy using the alias np.

docs.title: 3.1 Understanding Array Shapes¶
docs.text: The shape of an array is a tuple that gives you the size of the array in each dimension.

docs.title: 3.2 Reshaping Arrays (reshape)¶
docs.text: The reshape function allows you to change the shape of an array without changing its data.

docs.title: 3.3 Flattening Arrays (flatten and ravel)¶
docs.text:
Flattening an array converts it into a 1D array.

  • flatten returns a copy of the array collapsed into one dimension.
  • ravel returns a view (if possible) of the array collapsed into one dimension.

docs.title: 3.4 Transposing Arrays (transpose and T)¶
docs.text: Transposing an array swaps its dimensions.

docs.title: 4. Joining Arrays¶
docs.text: Joining or combining arrays allows you to merge multiple arrays into one.

docs.title: 4.1 Concatenation (concatenate)¶
docs.text: The concatenate function joins a sequence of arrays along an existing axis.

docs.title: Vertical Stack (vstack)¶
docs.text: Stacks arrays vertically (row-wise).

docs.title: Horizontal Stack (hstack)¶
docs.text: Stacks arrays horizontally (column-wise).

docs.title: Depth Stack (dstack)¶
docs.text: Stacks arrays along the third axis (depth).

docs.title: Generic Stack (stack)¶
docs.text: Stacks arrays along a new axis.

docs.title: 5. Splitting Arrays¶
docs.text: Splitting arrays allows you to divide an array into multiple sub-arrays.

docs.title: Split (split)¶
docs.text: Splits an array into multiple sub-arrays along a specified axis.

docs.title: Horizontal Split (hsplit)¶
docs.text: Splits an array horizontally (column-wise).

docs.title: Vertical Split (vsplit)¶
docs.text: Splits an array vertically (row-wise).

docs.title: Depth Split (dsplit)¶
docs.text: Splits an array along the depth (third) axis.

docs.title: 6. Adding and Removing Elements¶
docs.text: NumPy provides functions to insert, append, and delete elements in arrays.

docs.title: 6.1 Inserting Elements (insert)¶
docs.text: The insert function allows you to insert values into an array at specified indices.

docs.title: 6.2 Appending Elements (append)¶
docs.text: The append function adds values to the end of an array.

docs.title: 6.3 Deleting Elements (delete)¶
docs.text: The delete function removes elements at specified indices.

docs.title: 7. Copying and Viewing Arrays¶
docs.text: Understanding how copying works in NumPy is important to avoid unintended side effects.

docs.title: 7.1 No Copy at All¶
docs.text: Assigning an array to a new variable does not create a copy; both variables point to the same data.

docs.title: 7.2 View or Shallow Copy¶
docs.text: A view creates a new array object that looks at the same data.

docs.title: 7.3 Deep Copy¶
docs.text: A deep copy creates a new array and copies the data.

docs.title: NumPy Indexing and Slicing Arrays¶
docs.text: NumPy arrays (ndarray) are grid-like structures that can store data of the same type. They are similar to Python lists but offer faster computation and more efficient storage. Indexing and slicing are crucial for accessing and manipulating data within these arrays.

docs.title: Importing NumPy¶
docs.text: Before we begin, we need to import the NumPy library. It's a common practice to import NumPy using the alias np.

docs.title: 1D Array Indexing and Slicing¶
docs.text: One-dimensional (1D) arrays are the simplest form of NumPy arrays, similar to vectors. Indexing and slicing in 1D arrays work much like in standard Python lists.

docs.title: Indexing Individual Elements¶
docs.text: To access individual elements in a 1D array, you use square brackets [] with the index of the element. Remember that indexing starts at 0.

docs.title: Slicing Arrays¶
docs.text: Slicing allows you to access a range of elements in an array. The syntax for slicing is array[start:stop:step].

docs.title: 2D Array Indexing and Slicing¶
docs.text: Two-dimensional (2D) arrays are like matrices. Indexing and slicing in 2D arrays involve specifying row and column indices.

docs.title: Indexing Individual Elements¶
docs.text: To access an element in a 2D array, you provide two indices: one for the row and one for the column.

docs.title: Slicing Rows and Columns¶
docs.text: You can slice subsets of a 2D array by specifying ranges for rows and columns.

docs.title: Higher-Dimensional Arrays¶
docs.text: NumPy arrays can have more than two dimensions. The indexing and slicing principles extend naturally to higher dimensions.

docs.title: Conditional Selection¶
docs.text: Conditional selection allows you to select elements based on conditions rather than explicit indices. This is powerful for data analysis and preprocessing.

docs.title: Using Comparison Operators¶
docs.text: You can use comparison operators to create boolean arrays, which can then be used to index the array.

docs.title: Combining Conditions¶
docs.text: You can combine multiple conditions using logical operators such as & (and), | (or), and ~ (not).

docs.title: Boolean Indexing¶
docs.text: You can create a boolean array and use it to index your array.

docs.title: Advanced Indexing Techniques¶
docs.text: NumPy offers advanced indexing methods for more complex data selection.

docs.title: Integer Array Indexing¶
docs.text: You can use lists or arrays of integers to select multiple elements.

docs.title: Fancy Indexing¶
docs.text: Fancy indexing allows you to pass arrays of indices to select specific elements.

docs.title: Ellipsis (...) in Indexing¶
docs.text: The ellipsis ... is used to represent as many colons as needed to produce a complete indexing tuple.

docs.title: NumPy Basics: Statistical Functions¶
docs.text: NumPy provides a comprehensive suite of statistical functions that operate on arrays and matrices, allowing you to compute descriptive statistics, assess data distributions, and perform more complex analyses like correlation and covariance.

docs.title: Importing NumPy¶
docs.text: Before you begin working with NumPy's statistical functions, you need to import the library. It's a common practice to import NumPy using the alias np for convenience.

docs.title: Creating a Sample Dataset¶
docs.text: For demonstration purposes, let's create a sample NumPy array to work with. This array will simulate a dataset of numerical values.

docs.title: Basic Statistical Functions¶
docs.text: NumPy offers basic statistical functions that compute simple statistics like mean, median, sum, minimum, maximum, standard deviation, and variance.

docs.title: Mean (np.mean)¶
docs.text: The mean (average) is a measure of the central tendency of a dataset. You can calculate the mean of an array using the np.mean() function.

docs.title: Median (np.median)¶
docs.text: The median is the middle value of a sorted dataset. If the dataset has an even number of elements, the median is the average of the two middle numbers.

docs.title: Sum (np.sum)¶
docs.text: The sum function computes the total of all elements in the array.

docs.title: Min and Max (np.min, np.max)¶
docs.text: The np.min() and np.max() functions find the minimum and maximum values in the array, respectively.

docs.title: Standard Deviation and Variance (np.std, np.var)¶
docs.text: The standard deviation measures the amount of variation or dispersion in a dataset. The variance is the square of the standard deviation.

docs.title: Advanced Statistical Functions¶
docs.text: Beyond basic statistics, NumPy provides functions for more advanced statistical analysis, such as calculating percentiles, correlation coefficients, and covariance matrices.

docs.title: Percentiles (np.percentile)¶
docs.text: Percentiles are used to understand the distribution of data. The nth percentile is the value below which n% of the data falls.

docs.title: Correlation Coefficient (np.corrcoef)¶
docs.text: The correlation coefficient measures the linear relationship between two datasets. It returns a matrix of correlation coefficients between each pair of datasets.

docs.title: Covariance Matrix (np.cov)¶
docs.text: Covariance indicates the level to which two variables vary together. The covariance matrix shows the covariance between each pair of variables.

docs.title: Using the axis Parameter¶
docs.text:
Many statistical functions in NumPy accept an axis parameter, which specifies the axis along which to perform the computation.

  • axis=0: Compute along the columns (downward).
  • axis=1: Compute along the rows (across).

docs.text: NumPy's statistical functions can operate on multidimensional arrays. Let's explore how to apply these functions to 3D arrays.

docs.title: Introduction to Pandas: Creating Series and DataFrames¶
docs.text: Pandas is a powerful Python library used for data manipulation and analysis. It provides two primary data structures: Series and DataFrame. Understanding how to create and manipulate these structures is essential for data analysis tasks.

docs.title: Importing Pandas and NumPy¶
docs.text: Before we begin, we need to import the Pandas and NumPy libraries. NumPy is often used alongside Pandas for numerical operations.

docs.title: Pandas Series¶
docs.text: A Series is a one-dimensional labeled array capable of holding any data type (integers, strings, floating-point numbers, Python objects, etc.). Each element in a Series has an associated label, known as its index.

docs.title: Creating a Series from a List¶
docs.text: You can create a Series from a Python list by passing the list to the pd.Series() function.

docs.title: Creating a Series from a Dictionary¶
docs.text: A Series can also be created from a dictionary. The keys become the indices, and the values become the data.

docs.title: Creating a Series from a NumPy Array¶
docs.text: You can create a Series from a NumPy array in a similar way.

docs.title: Pandas DataFrame¶
docs.text: A DataFrame is a two-dimensional labeled data structure with columns that can be of different data types. It is similar to a spreadsheet or SQL table.

docs.title: Creating a DataFrame from a Dictionary¶
docs.text: You can create a DataFrame by passing a dictionary where the keys are column names and the values are lists of column data.

docs.title: Creating a DataFrame from a List of Dictionaries¶
docs.text: Sometimes, data is more naturally represented as a list of dictionaries, where each dictionary represents a row.

docs.title: Creating a DataFrame from a 2D NumPy Array¶
docs.text: You can also create a DataFrame from a 2D NumPy array by specifying the column names.

docs.title: Creating a DataFrame from Multiple Series¶
docs.text: You can create a DataFrame by combining multiple Series objects.

docs.title: Adding a Column¶
docs.text: You can add a new column to a DataFrame by assigning a Series or list to a new column name.

docs.title: Removing a Column¶
docs.text: To remove a column from a DataFrame, you can use the drop() method with axis=1.

docs.title: Accessing Columns and Rows¶
docs.text: You can access columns using the column name.

docs.title: Summary¶
docs.text:
• Series: One-dimensional labeled array. Created from lists, dictionaries, or NumPy arrays.
  • DataFrame: Two-dimensional labeled data structure. Created from dictionaries, lists of dictionaries, NumPy arrays, or multiple Series.
  • Manipulation: Add or remove columns, access data using labels or positions.

Understanding how to create and manipulate Series and DataFrames is fundamental when working with data in Pandas. These structures allow for efficient data analysis and manipulation, providing a foundation for more advanced operations.

docs.title: Basics of Pandas in Python: Aggregation & Groupby Methods¶
docs.text: Pandas is a powerful library in Python used for data manipulation and analysis. This tutorial will guide you through the basics of aggregation and groupby methods in Pandas, which are essential for summarizing and analyzing data.

docs.title: Aggregation Methods¶
docs.text: Aggregation involves computing a summary statistic (or statistics) about each group, which can include functions like mean, median, min, max, sum, count, etc.

docs.title: Creating a Sample DataFrame¶
docs.text: Let's start by creating a sample DataFrame that contains sales data for a fictional retail store. This data includes the Product ID, Category, Quantity Sold, and Revenue.

docs.title: Viewing the DataFrame¶
docs.text: Before we perform any aggregation, it's good practice to understand the structure of the DataFrame.

docs.title: Calculating Summary Statistics¶
docs.text: The describe() method generates descriptive statistics that summarize the central tendency, dispersion, and shape of a dataset’s distribution.

docs.title: Transposing the Summary Statistics¶
docs.text: Transposing the summary statistics can make them easier to read, especially when dealing with many columns.

docs.title: Calculating Specific Aggregations¶
docs.text: You can calculate specific aggregation metrics on individual columns.

docs.title: Mean¶
docs.text: Calculates the average value.

docs.title: Median¶
docs.text: Finds the middle value when the data is sorted.

docs.title: Mode¶
docs.text: Identifies the most frequently occurring value(s).

docs.title: Standard Deviation¶
docs.text: Measures the amount of variation or dispersion of a set of values.

docs.title: Variance¶
docs.text: Calculates how far the numbers are spread out from their average value.

docs.title: Sum¶
docs.text: Adds up all the values in a column.

docs.title: Product¶
docs.text: Calculates the product of all the values in a column.

docs.title: Groupby Methods¶
docs.text: Groupby involves splitting the data into groups based on some criteria, applying a function to each group independently, and then combining the results back together.

docs.title: Grouping Data¶
docs.text: Suppose we want to analyze the sales data by category.

docs.title: Mean by Group¶
docs.text: Calculates the average for each group.

docs.title: Sum by Group¶
docs.text: Calculates the total for each group.

docs.title: Min and Max by Group¶
docs.text: Finds the minimum and maximum values within each group.

docs.title: Grouping by Multiple Columns¶
docs.text: You can also group the data by multiple columns.

docs.title: Using the aggregate() Function¶
docs.text: The aggregate() function allows you to perform multiple aggregations on one or more columns.

docs.title: Applying Custom Functions¶
docs.text: You can apply custom functions to your groups using the apply() method.

docs.title: Combining Datasets in Pandas: Concatenating, Joining, and Merging¶
docs.text: In data analysis, we often need to combine datasets for a more comprehensive analysis. Pandas provides powerful methods for combining datasets: concatenating, joining, and merging. In this tutorial, we will cover these three methods with examples.

docs.title: Concatenation¶
docs.text: Concatenation involves stacking datasets either vertically (row-wise) or horizontally (column-wise). It is useful when you need to combine datasets with the same structure.

docs.title: Creating DataFrames for Concatenation¶
docs.text: We will start by creating three DataFrames with sales data from different months.

docs.title: Concatenating DataFrames Vertically (Row-wise)¶
docs.text: The pd.concat() function is used to concatenate DataFrames. By default, it concatenates row-wise.

docs.title: Concatenating DataFrames Horizontally (Column-wise)¶
docs.text: We can also concatenate the DataFrames column-wise by specifying axis=1.

docs.title: Merging¶
docs.text: Merging combines two DataFrames by matching rows based on one or more columns. This is particularly useful for linking datasets that have a common key.

docs.title: Creating DataFrames for Merging¶
docs.text: Let’s create two DataFrames that hold information about customers and their purchases.

docs.title: Merging with Inner Join (Default)¶
docs.text: The default merge type is an inner join, which returns rows where the values match in both DataFrames.

docs.title: Outer, Left, and Right Joins¶
docs.text:
Pandas supports different types of joins:

  • Outer Join: Includes all rows from both DataFrames, filling missing values with NaN.
  • Left Join: Includes all rows from the left DataFrame and matches from the right.
  • Right Join: Includes all rows from the right DataFrame and matches from the left.

docs.title: Merging on Multiple Columns¶
docs.text: Let’s create two more DataFrames with sales data to demonstrate merging on multiple columns.

docs.title: Joining¶
docs.text: Joining is used to combine DataFrames based on their index. It is ideal when you want to align datasets using the row labels.

docs.title: Inner and Outer Joins with Index¶

docs.title: Dealing with Missing Data in Pandas¶
docs.text: Real-world datasets often contain missing values, which can complicate data analysis. Pandas provides robust methods to handle missing data efficiently. In this tutorial, we'll explore how to identify, remove, and fill missing values in a Pandas DataFrame.

docs.title: Creating a DataFrame with Missing Data¶
docs.text: Let's start by creating a DataFrame that contains missing values. We'll use np.nan to represent missing entries.

docs.title: Identifying Missing Data¶
docs.text: Before we can handle missing data, we need to identify where it exists in our DataFrame.

docs.title: Using isnull()¶
docs.text: The isnull() function returns a DataFrame of boolean values indicating whether each value is missing.

docs.title: Using notnull()¶
docs.text: Similarly, the notnull() function returns True for non-missing values.

docs.title: Counting Missing Values¶
docs.text: We can calculate the total number of missing values in each column using the sum() function along with isnull().

docs.title: Removing Missing Values¶
docs.text: Sometimes, the simplest way to handle missing data is to remove it entirely.

docs.title: Dropping Rows with Missing Data¶
docs.text: To drop all rows that contain any missing values, use the dropna() function.

docs.title: Dropping Columns with Missing Data¶
docs.text: If you prefer to drop columns that contain missing values, set the axis parameter to 1.

docs.title: Filling Missing Values¶
docs.text: Often, we don't want to lose data by dropping rows or columns. Instead, we can fill missing values with appropriate substitutes.

docs.title: Using fillna()¶
docs.text: The fillna() function allows us to replace missing values with a specified value.

docs.title: Forward Fill (ffill)¶
docs.text: Forward fill replaces missing values with the last known value along a specified axis.

docs.title: Backward Fill (bfill)¶
docs.text: Backward fill uses the next valid observation to fill missing values.

docs.title: Filling with Mean, Median, or Mode¶
docs.text: For numerical columns, it's common to fill missing values with the mean, median, or mode.

docs.title: Filling with a Dictionary¶
docs.text: You can specify different fill values for different columns using a dictionary.

docs.title: How to Contribute to the AI Learning Hub 🛠️
docs.text: We’re thrilled that you’re interested in contributing to the AI Learning Hub! This guide will walk you through the steps to make your contributions seamless. Whether you’re submitting new tutorials, fixing bugs, or suggesting improvements, your efforts make a difference.

docs.title: Step 1: Familiarize Yourself with the Project
docs.text:
Before contributing, take some time to:

  • Explore the GitHub repository.
  • Understand the structure of the project and where your contribution fits.
  • Review any open issues or pull requests to avoid duplication.

docs.title: Step 2: Create or Select an Issue
docs.text:
1. Check for Existing Issues:

    • Browse the Issues section to see if your idea or task is already listed.
    • If you find an issue you'd like to work on, comment on it to let the maintainers know you're taking it up. Example comment: "I’d like to work on this issue. Please assign it to me!"

    • Create a New Issue:

    • If your contribution is new and not listed, create a detailed issue describing your idea or proposed feature.

    • Include as much information as possible, such as the content type, purpose, and scope.
    • Wait for approval from the maintainers before proceeding.

👉 Submit or Review Issues Here

docs.title: Step 3: Fork the Repository
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the AI Learning Hub GitHub repository.
  2. Click the Fork button in the top-right corner to create a personal copy of the repository.

docs.title: Step 4: Clone Your Fork
docs.text:
1. Open your terminal or command prompt.

  2. Clone your forked repository to your local machine by running:

    git clone https://github.com/<your-username>/ailearninghub.git

    Replace <your-username> with your GitHub username.

docs.title: Step 5: Set Up Your Development Environment
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the project directory:

    cd ailearninghub

  2. Create a virtual environment:

    python -m venv env

  3. Activate the virtual environment:

    • On Windows:

      .\env\Scripts\activate

    • On macOS/Linux:

      source env/bin/activate

  4. Install the required Python libraries:

    pip install -r requirements.txt

docs.title: Step 6: Make Your Changes
docs.text:
• Add or edit content, code, or documentation based on the approved issue or feature request.
  • Follow the existing project structure and style guides.
  • Test your changes locally to ensure everything works as expected.

docs.title: Creating Tutorials
docs.text:
1. Use the Python Basics Template: When creating a new tutorial, base your tutorial off the Python Basics tutorial located at:

    docs/ai_learning_roadmap/0_programming/python/basics.ipynb

    This ensures consistency in structure and formatting.

  2. Place Your Tutorial Correctly: Save your tutorial in the appropriate category and subdirectory, similar to how the Python Basics tutorial is structured.

  3. Add Your Tutorial to the mkdocs.yml File: Once your tutorial is created, you need to add it to the mkdocs.yml file for it to appear in the website navigation. Follow these steps:

    • Open the mkdocs.yml file in the root directory of the project.
    • Locate the section corresponding to your tutorial's category (e.g., Programming, Working with Data).

    • Add your tutorial under the appropriate subcategory, following the same format as the Python Basics file:

      - Programming:
    - "[Contribute]": 'ai_learning_roadmap/0_programming/contribute.md'
    - Python:
        - Basics: 'ai_learning_roadmap/0_programming/python/basics.ipynb'
        - Your Tutorial Title: 'path/to/your/tutorial/file.ipynb'

    • Use the example in the image below for guidance:

    • Ensure the file path matches the directory where your tutorial is saved.

docs.title: Step 7: Preview Your Changes Locally
docs.text:
Before creating a pull request, ensure your changes render correctly by using mkdocs:

  1. Start the development server:

    mkdocs serve

  2. Open the provided URL in your browser (usually http://127.0.0.1:8000) to preview your changes.

  3. Verify that everything looks and functions as expected.

docs.title: Step 8: Commit Your Changes
docs.text:
1. Stage your changes:

    git add .

  2. Commit your changes with a meaningful message:

    git commit -m "Add/Update [description of your changes]"

docs.title: Step 9: Push to Your Fork
docs.text:
Push your branch to your forked repository:

git push origin feature/your-feature-name

docs.title: Step 10: Create a Pull Request
docs.text:
1. Go to the original AI Learning Hub repository.
  2. Click the Pull Requests tab, then click New Pull Request.
  3. Select Compare Across Forks.
  4. Set the base repository to dankornas/ailearninghub and the compare repository to your fork.
  5. Add a clear title and description of your changes, referencing the approved issue number (e.g., "Fixes #42").
  6. Confirm that you’ve previewed your changes locally using mkdocs serve and include this note in your pull request description.
  7. Submit the pull request.

docs.title: Step 11: Collaborate and Refine
docs.text:
• The maintainers will review your pull request.
  • Be open to feedback and make necessary adjustments.

docs.title: Step 12: Celebrate Your Contribution! 🎉
docs.text: Once your pull request is merged, your contribution becomes part of the AI Learning Hub! Share your achievement with the community.

docs.title: Additional Tips
docs.text:
• Ask Questions: If you’re unsure about anything, ask in our Discord Community.

  • Be Respectful: Follow the Contributor Code of Conduct to ensure a welcoming environment for all contributors.

  • Stay Updated: Keep your fork in sync with the original repository by pulling updates regularly:

    git fetch upstream
git merge upstream/main

We’re excited to have you on board! Together, we’re building something extraordinary for the AI community.

docs.title: How to Create Tutorials for the AI Learning Hub 📝
docs.text: Thank you for contributing to the AI Learning Hub! This guide explains how to create tutorials that fit seamlessly into the project. By following these steps, we can maintain consistency, organization, and high-quality content.

docs.title: Step 1: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Before you start working on your tutorial:

  1. Create or Select an Issue: Ensure you’ve created or selected an issue in the GitHub Issues section and received approval to proceed.
  2. Set Up Your Environment: Follow the How to Contribute guide to set up your development environment, including installing dependencies and activating your virtual environment.

docs.title: Step 2: File Structure
docs.text:
After your issue has been approved and you’re ready to start, you’ll need to create a new file in the appropriate directory under ai-learning-roadmap. The directory structure is as follows:

docs/
└── ai-learning-roadmap/
    ├── 0_programming/
    ├── 1_working_with_data/
    ├── 2_machine_learning/
    ├── 3_deep_learning/
    └── 4_mlop_deployment/
  • Choose the directory that best matches your tutorial topic:
    • 0_programming: Tutorials on programming fundamentals like Python, algorithms, and basic data structures.
    • 1_working_with_data: Tutorials on working with data, including data cleaning, Pandas, NumPy, and visualization.
    • 2_machine_learning: Tutorials on machine learning models, algorithms, and workflows.
    • 3_deep_learning: Tutorials on neural networks, advanced AI techniques, and frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch.
    • 4_mlop_deployment: Tutorials on deploying machine learning models, pipelines, and MLOps best practices.

docs.title: Step 3: Working with Jupyter Notebooks
docs.text: The tutorials in this project will primarily be created using Jupyter Notebooks (.ipynb files). MkDocs-Jupyter will render these notebooks as interactive pages, so it’s important to follow formatting conventions to ensure proper rendering.

docs.title: How to Create and Save Your Notebook
docs.text:
1. Navigate to the directory where your tutorial will live (e.g., docs/ai-learning-roadmap/2_machine_learning).

  2. Open Jupyter Notebook or Jupyter Lab in your terminal:

    jupyter notebook

  3. Create a new notebook and save it with a descriptive name, such as:

    tutorial_name.ipynb

  4. Add your content using the structure outlined below.

docs.title: Step 4: Formatting Standards
docs.text: When using MkDocs-Jupyter, you’ll need to follow specific formatting conventions to ensure the notebook renders correctly. Here’s a breakdown:

docs.title: Markdown Cells
docs.text:
Use markdown cells for explanations, headings, and structured text. Below are some formatting guidelines:

  • Headings: Use markdown syntax for section headers.
    • # Main Title
    • ## Section Title
    • ### Subsection Title
  • Text Emphasis:
    • Italics: Surround text with single asterisks or underscores: _italic text_ or *italic text*
    • Bold: Surround text with double asterisks: **bold text**
    • Bold Italics: Combine both: ***bold italic text***

  • Bullet Points: Use - or * for unordered lists:

    - First item
- Second item

  • Numbered Lists: Use numbers for ordered lists:

    1. Step one
2. Step two

  • Links: Use [text](url) to create hyperlinks:

    [GitHub Repository](https://github.com/dankornas/ailearninghub)

  • Inline Code: Use backticks for inline code:

    Use `print()` to display output in Python.

docs.title: Code Cells
docs.text:
Use Python code cells for any programming examples or exercises. MkDocs-Jupyter renders these as executable cells. Ensure the following:

  1. Include relevant comments for clarity:

    # This function adds two numbers
def add(a, b):
    return a + b

  2. Provide input/output examples where possible:

    result = add(5, 10)
print(result)  # Output: 15

  3. Keep code concise and avoid overly complex examples.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
You can create tables in markdown cells for structured data:

| Parameter | Description     | Example  |
|-----------|-----------------|----------|
| Name      | The user's name | John Doe |
| Age       | User's age      | 25       |

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
Add images by linking them with markdown syntax:

![Alt Text](path/to/image.png)

docs.title: Tips and Notes
docs.text:
Use blockquotes for additional tips, notes, or warnings:

> **Note:** Ensure your Python version matches the required dependencies.

docs.title: Step 5: Add Author Information
docs.text: While creating your tutorial or immediately after, include a section at the end of your Jupyter notebook to provide information about yourself. This helps recognize contributors and builds a sense of community.

docs.title: Template for Author Information
docs.text:
At the end of your Jupyter notebook, add the following markdown cell:

---

## About the Author

This tutorial was created by **Your Name**.

- **GitHub**: [@your-github-username](https://github.com/your-github-username)
- **LinkedIn**: [Your LinkedIn Profile](https://linkedin.com/in/your-profile)
- **Twitter**: [@your-twitter-handle](https://twitter.com/your-twitter-handle) (optional)

If you have any questions or feedback, feel free to reach out or submit an issue in the [AI Learning Hub GitHub repository](https://github.com/dankornas/ailearninghub).

---

docs.title: Step 6: Content Guidelines
docs.text:
• Write tutorials in simple, clear, and engaging language.
  • Structure your tutorial into sections:
    1. Introduction: Briefly explain the topic and what learners will achieve.
    2. Prerequisites: List any tools, libraries, or knowledge needed.
    3. Step-by-Step Guide: Explain each step clearly with examples.
    4. Conclusion: Summarize the key takeaways and encourage further exploration.
  • Use real-world examples whenever possible to demonstrate practical applications.
  • Avoid overly long sections—break content into digestible chunks.

docs.title: Step 7: Testing and Previewing
docs.text:
Before submitting your tutorial:

  1. Run your Jupyter notebook end-to-end to ensure:
    • All code runs without errors.
    • Outputs match what’s expected.

  2. Use the mkdocs serve command to preview your tutorial locally:

    mkdocs serve

  3. Open the provided URL (usually http://127.0.0.1:8000) to verify formatting and readability.

docs.title: Step 8: Submit Your Tutorial
docs.text:
Once your tutorial is complete and tested:

  • Commit your changes with a descriptive message.
  • Create a pull request and link it to your issue.
  • Be open to feedback from maintainers to refine your work.

Thank you for contributing to the AI Learning Hub and helping us create a world-class learning resource! 🚀
